title: Electrochemical training of nanoporous Cu-In catalysts for efficient CO2-to-CO conversion and high durability
abstract: Electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction into valuable chemicals is usually implemented at high overpotential, and most bimetallic catalysts suffer from the dramatic evolution of surface composition especially in case of long-term operation. In this work, as a proof-of-concept experiment, one effective protocol is first identified to drive the positive evolution of surface contents on nanoporous Cu-In by electrochemical training in KHCO3 electrolyte. Interestingly, superior performances including high selectivity for CO production and robust reliability are realized. Thus, Faradaic efficiency can approach the maximum of 91% at −0.95 V (vs. RHE), and an excellent durability can be simultaneously testified by no detectable performance decay for 7 hours in operation. More importantly, current investigation paves a new road for designing bimetallic electrocatalysts with high selectivity and long-term durability.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
One way to relieve the surging consumption of fossil energy is to accomplish electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction (CDR) toward valuable chemicals and fuels.[1–3] However, thermodynamic stability of CO2 molecules and sluggish reaction kinetics require the rational design of high performance electrocatalysts.[4] Recently, nanostructured metals have continuously been attracting much attention owing to their ability to offer excellent activity and distinct selectivity during the CDR compared to their bulk counterparts.[5] So far, monometallic catalysts have been developed to facilitate CO2 conversion into CO and formic acid on Au, Ag, Pd, Sn and Bi nanostructures.[4,6] Among various metallic electrocatalysts used as cathodes, copper enables reducing CO2 into various hydrocarbons,[7] owing to its moderate binding strength with CO, a major intermediate during the CDR, in favor of its further reduction into appreciable C1-C2 products.[8] Centi and co-workers have recently demonstrated the role of small Cu nanoparticles deposited on carbon nanotubes in influencing the C-C coupling, thus producing liquid products with high conversion efficiency.[9] Besides size effect,[10] overall catalysis can be also optimized by manipulating some geometric parameters, such as atomic coordination,[11] surface facet,[12] and strain level[13,14] in these monometallic nanostructures.
However, the refined tuning on these nanostructures exhibits the limitation in tuning their electronic structures to simultaneously enhance the CDR and inhibit hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), a competing side reaction at high overpotential. To address this issue, many previous investigations have attempted to adjust electronic structures by incorporating extraneous transition metals to fabricate bimetallic systems. As a result, tuning the adsorption energy of key intermediate species for different reactions independently becomes possible in experiment, providing a spacious room for selectivity enhancement.[15] So far, catalytic selectivity and activity have been considered in Pd-Au,[16] Cu-Pt,[17] Ag-Sn,[18] Cu-Sn,[19] Cu-In,[20] CuAg,[21] and Fe-Cu.[22] nanostructures. Among them, Cu-Sn and Cu-In nanostructures are two kinds of model electrocatalysts because the minor Sn or In soluted into Cu lattice brings about the CO with high FE. The selectivity of these alloying nanostructures exhibits the complete distinction relative to Cu nanoparticles, inducing the production of various hydrocarbon products.[19,20] However, structural instability of these alloy catalysts becomes the major obstacle for precise control on catalytic selectivity, especially in cases of long-term operation and

For bimetallic electrocatalysts, surface composition at atomic scale becomes paramount importance, which significantly influences the selectivity.[23,24] So far, few studies focus on the evolution of extraneous elements onto the bimetallic catalyst surface during the CDR. Herein, we experimentally demonstrate kinetic evolution of surface contents on nanoporous Cu-In (np-Cu-In) electrocatalyst, in accompany with positive effect on catalytic activity and selectivity.

sections.heading: 2.1. Catalyst fabrications
sections.text:
To prepare alloying precursor, Al (99.99%), Cu (99.999%) and In (99.99%) were used as received from Sinopham Chemical. The aluminum-copper-indium (Al73Cu25In2,) ternary precursors were prepared by an arc melting furnace under argon atmosphere at a pressure of 4.8×10-4 Pa (Anhui Jiao Shuo Incorporation, China). The alloy ingots were subsequently solidified rapidly by single roller melt-spinning into the ribbons with a thickness of 15-20 µm. The np-Cu-In was made by chemical dealloying of the precursor by corroding the ribbon in 5 wt.% HCl solution at room temperature for 24 hours.[25,26] The resultant nanoporous product was rinsed by deionized water and alcohol in sequential order to remove residual chemicals. Nanoporous sample was attached on copper tape as current collector, and the marginal region uninterested was sealed by the silicone in favor of calculating geometrical area of the electrode.
2.2 Electrochemical training of the np-Cu-In
One electrode was used during electrochemical training in order to get the comparable FECO and partial current densities. The detailed characterizations of catalytic stability, Raman spectra, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were conducted on the different electrodes. These electrodes were trained in the electrolyte by performing a pretreatment, making sure the occurrence of surface reconstruction.

Every compartment contained 25 ml of electrolyte that we typically purged with a high-purity carbon dioxide (Xiangyun Gas Incorporations, 99.995%) for at least 30 minutes prior to the electrolysis. Platinum mesh was used as the counter electrode, and a saturated Hg/HgCl was utilized as reference electrode. We used a CHI 660E potentiostat to apply all potentials. The measured potentials were then converted to the potential vs RHE by using E (versus RHE)=E (vs Hg/HgCl )+0.0591×pH+0.2419 V. Gas products were conducted into the Gas Chromatography (GC, FULI 9790II, Fuli Analytical Instrument Co. Ltd, China) automatically using an Arduino intelligent peristaltic pump (BT100LC) at a constant speed of 67 rpms with gas flow rate of 10 mL/s for 6 minutes. The GC was fitted with a packed molecular sieve 5A column and a packed Hayesep D column, in which Argon (Praxair, 99.999%) was utilized as the carrier gas. In addition, the GC equipped by two detectors, namely flame ionization detector (FID) attached with a methanizer was used to quantify CO concentration, and the thermal conducting detector (TCD) that was used to quantify H2 concentration. Gas products in the column passed through the TCD for the measurement of H2, and then they flowed into a methanizer where CO is converted to methane for the subsequent measurement in the FID detector. In our experiment, detection limit for CO and H2 was 10 and 100 ppm, respectively. Faradaic efficiency is estimated by detecting the concentrations of gas productions from the integrated area of GC peak. Therefore the instantaneous partial current densities were given by jCO = FECO × jtot, where jCO is partial current density for CO, FECO is the Faradaic efficiency for CO product, and jtot is total current density normalized by geometrical surface area of the catalyst. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) was done under same electrolyte saturated by carbon dioxide. In order to quantify the liquid products, a 0.5 mL electrolyte was mixed with 0.1 µL of Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9%) which was added as an internal standard and 0.1 mL Deuterium oxide ultra-D (D2O, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9%). A sample portion of the overall mixture was then tested by a Bruker AscendTM 500WB Nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussions
sections.text:
The precursor consists of multiple phases including α-Al, metallic In, and Al2Cu that are revealed by the XRD patterns in Fig. 1a. After chemical dealloying, three sharp peaks marked with solid circle are assigned to (111), (200) and (220) of metallic Cu. Two additional peaks marked with open circles are assigned to (111) and (220) of the Cu2O, indicating partial oxidation on the as-prepared nanoporous sample after air exposure.[19,27] Although metallic In is not detected in nanoporous sample in XRD pattern, In element with a concentration of 6.7% is verified by the EDS in Fig. 1b, implying that the In atoms are diluted into Cu lattices as the solute. SEM image in Fig. 1c represents the hierarchically porous channels that are spatially interconnected.[26] Larger pores with a channel width of 90-140 nm, appear like a maze, and the elongated geometries in the other direction can exceed one micron throughout the electrode. In comparison, some small pores on the maze wall are estimated as 50 nm, showing the comparable scale to the ligaments in Fig. 1d. According to previous investigations, large pores usually facilitate mass transport within hollow channels,[20, 28] whereas the small pores substantially increases surface area, providing more active sites for the electrocatalysis. Therefore, such hierarchically porous structure is normally believed to be advantageous for the overall performance of the CDR.[25,29,30]
The as-prepared np-Cu-In was firstly trained for different durations at the constant potential in order to attain the stable catalysis. Fig. 2a represents the temporal evolution of partial current density for CO production (jCO). At lower potential of -0.45 V versus RHE, the jCO exhibits a gradual climbing during the seven hours electrolysis. Upon increase of the constant potential from -0.45 to -0.95 V, the jCO saturates at higher level after the electrolysis for seven hours. At - 0.95 V, the jCO exhibits seven times enhancement after the entire electrolysis. Different from

temporal evolution of the jCO, the jH2 shows a reverse tendency in the same electrochemical parameters as shown in Fig. 2b.
The reverse tendencies of temporal dependence of current density between the jCO and the jH2 actually indicate selectivity enhancement on the np-Cu-In.[20] Usually, the CDR and HER performances rely on microstructural evolution of the catalysts, which might be identified by SEM observations and spectroscopic characterizations. Fig. S1 indicates the surface morphology of the np-Cu-In after seven hours electrolysis at -0.95 V, indicating negligible change in ligament geometry and pore size in comparison with the as-prepared np-Cu-In.
Moreover, the surface restructuring was subsequently investigated by in-situ redox behaviors of indium or its oxides before, during and after seven hours of stabilization by cyclic the CV sweeps in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution as depicted in Fig. 2c. Both In and Cu redox peaks occur within the CV scanned potential window (as shown in Fig. 2c). The cathodic peak around -0.34 V vs. RHE accompanied by its right shifted anodic peak are attributed to the reduction of indium oxide, while the cathodic peaks at around 0.6 V correspond to the reduction of Cu2O.[24] The temporal reduction of indium oxide during the CDR is integrated as shown in Fig. 2d. The integrated area increases steadily and displays four times enhancement after seven hours CDR which actually depicts the enrichment of In elements on the Cu-skeleton during the CDR process. The In enrichment phenomenon was also verified by the EDS in Fig. S2, showing larger atomic percentage of In elements on the np-Cu-In after 7 hours training. Fig. S3 shows TEM image of the np-Cu-In after electrochemical training, which shows additional surface roughness. HRTEM was done on the trained np-Cu-In in order to elucidate microstructural changes at nm scale. As represented in Fig. 3a, indium oxide islands are visible on the ligament surface. This hints structural evolution into Cu-rich core with oxide shell catalyst leading to overall activity improved. To further uncover intrinsic mechanism of selectivity enhancement, Raman spectra are collected to identify surface composition of the np-Cu-In prior to and after CDR (They are assigned as np-Cu-In-1 and np-Cu-In-2, respectively) as shown in Fig. 3b. The np-Cu-In-1 shows Raman bands at 146 and 218 cm-1, corresponding to the Cu-O vibration modes when the sample is exposed in the air.[31,32] The weak Raman band at 125 cm-1 is identified as the In-O vibration mode.[33,34] For the np-Cu-In-2, the Cu-O vibration modes at 146 and 218 cm-1 disappear completely, implying the complete reduction of copper oxide into

metallic copper during the CDR, which shows the identical spectra to the references.[31,35] Interestingly, the intensity of In-O vibration mode holds a significant enhancement accompanied with a slight shift from 125 to 124 cm-1 after the electrolysis for seven hours. According to the redox of the np-Cu-In as shown in Fig. 2c, the In2O3 should be reduced into metallic In at around -0.34 V vs RHE. Essentially, the In2O3 cannot survive in the Cu-In electrode at -0.95 V vs RHE that is much lower than its reduction potential. Therefore, Raman intensity of In2O3 originates from natural oxidization of the enriched In elements in the atmosphere. In the np-Cu-In-2, stronger Raman intensity can result from surface enrichment of In elements after electrochemical training in comparison with the np-Cu-In-1.
These detailed analysis on Raman spectra implies the enrichment of indium element onto ligament surface, which can also be confirmed by surface analysis technique.[24] The XPS in Fig. S4 exhibits a wide survey spectrum of the np-Cu-In, with the appearances of Cu and In elements as our expectation. On the other hand, Fig. 3c represents the comparable peak position of Cu2p 1/2 or Cu2p3/2, which are the dominant features of metallic copper.[36] The XPS spectrum of the np-Cu-In-1 in Fig. 3d shows the binding energies at 444.56 eV and 452.15 eV, corresponding to In3d5/2 and In3d3/2 electronic states. The In3d3/2 and In3d5/2 peaks on the np-CuIn-2 show a slight shift of ~0.41 eV toward higher binding energy with respect to the np-Cu-In-1. Meanwhile, peak intensities on the np-Cu-In-2 exhibit four-fold increase relative to the np-CuIn-1, implying that the surface is composed of more In atoms compared to Cu atoms after the CDR.
After getting the saturated CO FE on the np-Cu-In-2, the CDR is carried out at different potentials as shown in Fig. 4a. At -0.65V vs. RHE, the H2 FE is ~6%, while the CO FE is ~74%. The CO FE increases monotonously with the reduction potential, so that maximum value of 91% is obtained at -0.95 V. Besides gas products collected on the np-Cu-In-2, the liquid products can be obtained from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrum in Fig. S5. As it can be seen, formic acid is the only product in the liquid, and its concentration decreases with the decreasing potential from a maximum FE of 22% at -0.65 V to an undetectable level at -1.05 V. The potential corresponding to maximum CO production is about 0.35 V lower than that on Cu-In nanostructures or their derivatives as listed in Table 1. Usually, the overpotential is very sensitive to the activation of CO2 molecules on catalyst surface that is the rate determining step during the

CDR according to theoretical and experimental investigations. [4,20,23] Charge transfer between the catalyst and CO2 molecules usually depends on localized microstructures and compositions at active site. In our experiments, surface enrichment of In elements after electrochemical training probably affects the adsorption and activation of CO2 molecules, showing different behaviors with Cu-In alloy and In thin film reported in previous investigations.[20,23,24] To clarify the mechanism of activation behavior at the interfaces, a Tafel plot of CO partial current density (log jCO) against overpotential (η) was represented in Fig. 4b. A Tafel slope of 102 mV/dec indicates that the activation of CO2 molecules is the rate-determining step for metallic electrode via the formation of CO2 * intermediate by the initial e- transfer step at low overpotential less than 0.4 V.[6,38]
In order to gain insight on the reliability of catalytic selectivity, the the np-Cu-In-2 after electrochemical training was conducted for the CDR at a constant potential of -0.95 V as displayed in Fig. 4c. The CO FE of ~91% is obtained throughout seven hours, while H2 FE below 6% as well as formic acid at 3% is obtained with a steady current density of ~ 4.5mA/cm2. This finding suggests that trace amount of indium on Cu surface is responsible for inducing the enhanced selectivity toward CO. Therefore, surface composition and catalytic performance becomes stable after electrochemical training of the catalysts. The steady CDR performance on our nanoporous catalyst is compared to previous results on different Cu-In catalysts as summarized in Table 1, showing the highest level.
To understand intrinsic mechanism of the enhanced selectivity on the np-Cu-In-2, we can
analyze possible evolution of its surface compositions or structures after electrochemical training. One possibility to change surface composition is the direct deposition of minor metals by electrochemical reduction of the contaminated ions in the electrolyte, such as Pb, Ca, Fe and Mg etc. To rule out this possible effect, we conducted electrochemical training of nanoporous Cu without indium solute in the same electrolyte and checked its catalytic performance of the CDR. However, both CO and H2 FEs on nanoporous Cu in Fig.S6 do not increase with training time, implying that minor deposition of trace ions hardly makes the dominant contribution to catalytic selectivity. The other possibility to change surface composition is indium enrichment after electrochemical training, which is verified by redox of indium, Raman spectrum and XPS as described before. Surface reconstructions like this are frequently observed in some alloying

nanostructures, which are subjected to chemical reaction including heterogeneous catalysis and electrochemical catalysis.[39,40] Anisotropic segregation of Pt atoms toward the corners in nanoporous Ni-Pt frame during chemical synthesis in the solution.[40] Cyclic voltammetry of nanoporous Au-Pt-Pd for tens of cycles during oxygen reduction reaction shows the rearrangements of Pt and Pd atoms on the surface, with the subsequent shift of on-set potential.[41]
In our experiments, the as-prepared np-Cu-In includes Cu2O and Cu-In solid solute, and the Cu2O is potentially reduced into metallic Cu at the potential of the CDR, which is confirmed by complete disappearances of its Raman bands at 146 and 218 cm-1 as shown in Fig. 3b. Secondly, indium concentration on the np-Cu-In catalyst shows the monotonous increase according to insitu electrochemical redox of the indium in the KHCO3 electrolyte as shown in Fig. 2c and 2d. Therefore, the enrichment of indium species on the np-Cu-In-2 is also evidenced by the stronger signal of Raman band at 124 cm-1. Usually, most indium oxide cannot survive during the CDR, especially at high overpotential. According to previous investigations, metallic indium onto catalyst surface rather than indium oxide is believed to make the dominant contribution to catalytic selectivity for CO production, especially for the indium-rich surface.[24,43]
Therefore, how can we correlate the reconstructed surface in the np-Cu-In-2 with superior selectivity for CO production? In principle, catalytic selectivity is well related to enhance the target reaction (CDR) and inhibit the HER by considering the adsorption behavior of their corresponding intermediates on the catalysts. In the np-Cu-In-2, indium enrichment onto the surface might change adsorption behaviors of some chemical species, such as *H, and *COOH, which are the key intermediates for H2 and CO productions, respectively.[14,24] For alloying surface of the np-Cu-In, the d orbital of Cu atoms coupled with the p orbital of In atoms may enable modulating adsorption energy of the *COOH. The simulation based on density functional theory indicates that In atoms on various alloying surfaces could reduce the number of multi-fold sites with strong adsorption ability. For the *COOH, In atoms localized onto Cu surface can improve the stability of *COOH by roughly 0.1 eV, [20] with a result of the inhibited release of *COOH in favor of its further reduction into CO. The stronger adsorption energy of the *COOH on the In actually indicates that its CO2-to-CO conversion efficiency should be improved after

Besides the enhanced activity of the CDR on the np-Cu-In-2, high CO2-to-CO conversion might be obtained when the HER is inhibited due to the weaken adsorption of the *H. The jH2 in Fig. 2b indicates the monotonous declination when indium aggregation becomes serious with electrochemical training. Therefore, both the enhanced CDR and the inhibited HER in the npCu-In-2 catalyst should make the overall contribution to catalytic selectivity toward CO, resulting in a superior selectivity of 91% at -0.95 V.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text: In summary, composition evolution of surface structures in alloying catalysts is a crucial issue that affects the catalytic activity, selectivity and durability for the CDR. In this work, we reported the fabrication of the Cu-In solid solution with the hierarchically porous structures. When the npCu-In is trained by the CDR procedure at different potentials, the indium enrichment occurs onto ligament surfaces, which is experimentally identified by Raman spectroscopy and electrochemical redox. Different from the deteriorated selectivity on most alloying catalysts, the overall performance on np-Cu-In exhibits an enhanced selectivity for CO production and the inhibited HER when indium enrichment occurs on the surface. Consequently, CO2-to-CO converting efficiency can be as high as 91% at -0.95 V vs RHE. Experimental demonstration on the enhanced performance in electrochemical environments offers one avenue to design bimetallic catalysts with excellent catalysis and durability at high overpotential.
